newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION-From the Beehive-Muted welcome for BPS.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-From the Beehive-Muted welcome for BPS.

text.p: WELLINGTON, March 5 - New Zealand Treasurer Winston Peters has worked hard at transforming himself from devil to angel in the eyes of the financial markets.

But despite his new-found fiscal and monetary conservatism the reaction to his first major set piece -- Tuesday's Budget Policy Statement, giving a broad brush look at June's Budget -- was less than enthusiastic.
It started with the media, who were peeved at having to question Peters after a short speech but before they viewed the BPS itself.
Finance Minister Bill Birch's had always arrived after journalists had spent some time with the document.

Peters' way led to speculation he did not want to answer the tough questions or was not on top of the material -- a view reinforced by his answers to questions which included a refusal to detail priorities, even though they were in the BPS, and a rambling personal view on debt reduction even though there were major changes to the government's short and long term plans.
Economists with a longer-term focus were also concerned at the implicit rise in spending, partly disguised in the tighter fiscal position in the 1997/98 year.

Moving $250 million in spending from year one to year three was explained by the time it would take to get programmes running, but earlier hints from treasury ministers suggested it was also because the full coalition programme would cost more than the cap placed on it.

While the $5 billion cap remains on the three-year programme -- and for a parliament with a three-year term it is reasonable to project over that period -- the long-term impact is a baseline $250 million higher from the year 2000 than the coalition document foresaw.

While noting that the $5 billion spending and the planned tax cuts were at the "upper limit" of prudence, Treasury's dries may have preferred this "cake later" approach. As economic and fiscal outcomes alter, the recipe can always be changed. Cake consumed is irretrievable.

Will the chef be back in the kitchen? Growth predictions in the DEFU of 3-3.5 percent over the next three years were not recast for the BPS and are looking increasingly optimistic. They provide the engine room of revenues and cap welfare costs.

The BPS notes that recent economic data suggest growth is slowing but at 2.3 percent in the September 1996 year, remained strong. The coalition agreeement did not change its view of potential growth, although precise details could. It said higher growth in 1998/99 would be offset by lower average growth later. Politically, extra spending, if it is manageable, will come in useful for New Zealand First in election year 1999-2000.

There was always a concern in New Zealand First that its impact, what Peters calls "the difference", would be evident early in the term in the details of the coalition agreement but would wane in voters' minds closer to the election.

Peters risks not delivering the full programme if the economy slows, although the BPS states: "The government is unlikely to change its revenue and expenses settings in the event of temporary divergences from the economic forecasts."
Then there is the referendum on compulsory superannuation.
If it delivers a yes' vote in September the government wants to cut taxes to compensate and to lessen the impact of a reduction in spending power.

NZ First policy was for an initial three percent contribution in 1998-99 to be balanced by the deferred $1.1 billion tax cut from 1997/98. Another two percent would be added in 1999/2000 and then one percent in each of the next three years to reach eight percent.
The coalition document envisaged another $1 billion in tax cuts in the 1999/2000 year to compensate for the second round of contributions, but the BPS puts that severely in doubt.
In a note in the BPS, Treasury said the cut was contingent on the availability of adequate surpluses and a positive vote in the referendum, so it was not included in the projections.
Already the DEFU projections for the operating balance in 1999/2000 have been slashed from $6.1 billion to $3.45 billion and would go down to $2.45 billion if the cut was introduced.
Its conditionality, and that of tax reductions further out, leaves the question of what the government plans if there is a yes vote and an economic downturn that does not leave "adequate surpluses".
It seems the compulsion to save would go ahead without the compensatory tax cuts.
(Note - the opinions expressed are those of the author and should not be taken to represent the views of Reuters).
